conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in postpartum emotional health. I’m here to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve in this new season of motherhood.

I’d like to spend the next few minutes doing a quick screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s a short, 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past week. It isn’t a test of your parenting or a label—it’s simply a way for us to listen to your experience and make sure we’re offering the right kind of help.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell us there’s an immediate safety concern. We want you to feel safe, heard, and supported.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no need to over-think, just tell me what feels true for you. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

I used to laugh really easily—my husband and I would joke around all the time—but this week it’s been… well, it’s been hard. Mostly I feel too tired or tense to find things funny. A couple of times something small made me smile, but it didn’t last.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No… not really. I mean, I smiled once when the baby made a silly face, but it felt forced. Mostly I’m too worn out or worried to laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much lately. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk—but now it feels like I’m just getting through the day. I still try to plan stuff, but the “looking forward” part feels flat, like I’m doing it because I should, not because I expect to enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I’m not feeding him properly or I missed some cue. Yesterday he wouldn’t nap and I kept replaying everything I’d done, convinced it was my fault for not reading him correctly. Even when my partner says the baby is fine, I still feel like I’m failing somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. My mind keeps jumping to the worst-case scenarios—like if he coughs I’m scared it’s pneumonia, or if he sleeps a little longer I’m sure something’s wrong. I know it’s probably nothing, but I can’t stop checking his breathing or Googling symptoms. It’s exhausting but I can’t seem to shut it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week, yeah. Nothing dramatic, just this sudden tight-chest feeling—like I’m bracing for something awful to happen to the baby even when everything looks fine. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and watching the monitor all night.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. Between the night feedings, the laundry pile, and trying to keep the baby settled, it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. I start one chore, hear him cry, rush over, and by the time I get back I’ve forgotten what I was doing. I keep telling myself “just keep swimming,” but yeah—it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I finally get him down, but then my head starts spinning with all the “what-ifs” and the mental to-do list. I’ll lie there for an hour or two, and even when I do drift off I jolt awake at every tiny sound, sure he’s up again. I’m running on maybe four broken hours a night, and it’s wearing me down.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time, yeah. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that just hangs over the day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason. I keep thinking I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’ve got help—but the sadness keeps leaking through anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times this week. Yesterday I just sat in the rocker with him asleep on my chest and started crying because everything felt so heavy. I couldn’t even explain why—I just felt overwhelmed and empty at the same time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again and be a good mom.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant approx. ≤ 3 mo) – self-report on EPDS-10 analogue

Symptoms / Concerns
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt over routine infant care  
- Marked anxiety (generalized & situational), intrusive catastrophic worries, nocturnal hypervigilance  
- Two discrete panic-equivalent episodes (chest tightness, fear something bad imminent)  
- Sleep disruption secondary to ruminating & infant monitoring (≈ 4 hrs fragmented/night)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed, “drowning,” poor concentration/forgetfulness  
- Denies self-harm ideation (score 0 on Q10)

Pattern
Consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depressive & anxiety symptoms, functionally impairing.

Screening Significance
EPDS-style scoring: 0-1-2-3 on each item → provisional total ≥ 16 (high threshold). High endorsement on core depressive items (Q8, Q9, Q2, Q1) and anxiety items (Q4, Q5, Q3). Meets DSM-5-TR “red-flag” level for further evaluation of Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset and comorbid Anxiety Disorder.

Risk Factors
- Depressive cognitions, guilt, hopelessness  
- Anxiety-driven safety behaviors (repeated checking, Googling)  
- Severe sleep deprivation amplifying mood liability  
- No protective suicidal ideation reported; no psychotic features elicited

Observation
Patient demonstrates clinically significant postpartum mood/anxiety symptoms that exceed “baby blues” threshold; immediate comprehensive assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, clinician interview) and appropriate level of care recommended. Safety plan reviewed; no current self-harm risk.
